title: Social Cognitive Learning in Early Childhood Islamic Prayer Education
affiliation: Postgraduate Programme in Early Childhood Islamic Education, Universitas Islam Negeri Fatmawati Sukarno Bengkulu, Bengkulu, Indonesia
abstract: Early childhood Islamic education requires teaching that connects observation, recall, supported practice, and motivation. This study describes the application of a social cognitive approach to daily supplications and prayer recitation at RA Plus JÃ¢-alHaq, Bengkulu. A qualitative descriptive design combined classroom observation, semi-structured interviews, and documentation during Marchâ€“April 2026. Group B2 was the principal observation group, while Group B1 supplied supporting information. Analysis used data reduction, display, and verification, supported by source and technique triangulation. The findings identify teacher modelling, repeated recitation, practical demonstration, and positive reinforcement as interconnected instructional practices. In B2, 18 of 21 children were rated at or above expected development for daily supplication, while reported attainment varied across the supporting group and prayer tasks. These distributions describe classroom attainment rather than preâ€“post gains. The study contributes a contextual account of how attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation are enacted in everyday religious learning. The findings suggest that task-specific observation, patient assistance, and consistent adult examples are central to developmentally responsive religious teaching.

title: Teacher Strategies for Improving Learning Quality in an Integrated Islamic Kindergarten
affiliation: Postgraduate Programme in Early Childhood Islamic Education, Universitas Islam Negeri Fatmawati Sukarno Bengkulu, Bengkulu, Indonesia
abstract: Improving kindergarten learning requires coordination between developmentally appropriate teaching, institutional support, and family participation. This study describes teachersâ€™ strategies for improving learning quality at TK IT Mutiara Cendekia, Lubuklinggau, and examines the conditions supporting and constraining their implementation. A qualitative descriptive design was employed during Aprilâ€“May 2026. Data were collected through observation, interviews, and documentation involving one principal, four teachers, and four parents. Analysis followed data reduction, data display, and conclusion verification, with source triangulation used to compare perspectives. The findings identify an interconnected strategy comprising flexible planning, play and learning centres, differentiated assistance, concrete learning materials, Islamic habituation, continuous assessment, and parent communication. Teachers adapted activities to childrenâ€™s interests, developmental differences, and fluctuating attention. Professional development, leadership, and a supportive environment facilitated implementation, while limited media variety and uneven family participation remained constraints. The study contributes a contextual account of how classroom adaptation and organisational support operate together. These findings describe perceived and observed improvements in learning processes rather than statistically established intervention effects.

title: Snack-Waste Collage Media to Improve Fine Motor Skills in Early Childhood
affiliation: Postgraduate Programme in Early Childhood Islamic Education, Universitas Islam Negeri Fatmawati Sukarno Bengkulu, Bengkulu, Indonesia
abstract: Fine motor competence is essential for childrenâ€™s readiness to write, manipulate learning materials, and perform daily tasks independently, yet classroom stimulation is often repetitive and underuses materials available in the surrounding environment. This study aimed to develop snack-waste collage media and examine its feasibility, practicality, and effectiveness in improving the fine motor skills of children aged five to six years at TK Hang Tuah, Bengkulu. The study employed a research and development design using the ADDIE model. The analysed assessment tables contained 18 Group B children; a classroom teacher and media and language validators contributed product appraisals. Data were collected through needs observation, expert-validation sheets, a teacher-response questionnaire, documentation, and pretest and posttest fine-motor assessment records. The media-expert score increased from 66.7% during the first validation to 95.8% after revision, while language validation was reported as 95.8%; conflicting teacher-response percentages prevented confirmation of a single practicality score. Recalculated tabulated scores increased from 52.55% to 88.66%, a gain of 36.11 percentage points, pending reconciliation with the original assessment sheets. The findings indicate that carefully cleaned and prepared snack packaging can provide attractive, economical, and environmentally meaningful collage material that supports hand-eye coordination, finger control, accuracy, and task completion in early childhood learning.

title: Internalising Nine Character Pillars Through Clapping Games in Early Childhood Education
affiliation: Postgraduate Programme in Early Childhood Islamic Education, Universitas Islam Negeri Fatmawati Sukarno Bengkulu, Bengkulu, Indonesia
abstract: Character education in early childhood requires activities that connect moral language with participation and everyday conduct. This study examines how clapping games supported the introduction and initial internalisation of nine character pillars at TK Barunawati, Bengkulu. A qualitative descriptive design was used during the second semester of the 2025/2026 academic year. Data were gathered through classroom observation, semi-structured interviews, and documentation, with teachers and children selected for their involvement in the activities. Analysis involved data reduction, narrative display, and conclusion drawing. The findings show that researcher-designed chants combined short value statements, movement, rhythm, modelling, and repetition across opening, main, and closing activities. Children recalled phrases, coordinated with peers, and sometimes initiated or led the games. Younger children experienced greater difficulty synchronising words and movements and required slower demonstrations. The study contributes a process account of transforming clapping from an incidental classroom energiser into intentional character learning. Given the approximately one-month implementation and absence of longitudinal assessment, the findings indicate engagement and emerging understanding rather than established, enduring character change.

title: Raudhatul Athfal Teachersâ€™ Perceptions of a Love Based Curriculum in Bengkulu
affiliation: Postgraduate Programme in Early Childhood Islamic Education, Universitas Islam Negeri Fatmawati Sukarno Bengkulu, Bengkulu, Indonesia
abstract: Curriculum change depends partly on how teachers interpret its purposes and translate them into classroom practice. This study examines Raudhatul Athfal teachersâ€™ perceptions of a love-based curriculum in Bengkulu, focusing on understanding, acceptance, and implementation readiness. A qualitative descriptive design combined semi-structured interviews, observation, and documentation. Sites were selected through a staged lottery across three districts; the findings draw on educator accounts from eight Raudhatul Athfal. Data were analysed through reduction, display, and verification, with source and technique triangulation. Teachers generally valued compassion, empathy, emotional safety, and character formation, but differed in how they understood the curriculumâ€™s relationship with Kurikulum Merdeka. Some perceived a useful reinforcement of existing practice, while others questioned the need for change. Limited and uneven training, administrative demands, facilities, and parental expectations constrained readiness. The study contributes an account of the gap between agreement with curricular values and confidence in implementation. The findings support staged, practice-oriented professional learning and clarification of curricular integration, while not establishing the curriculumâ€™s effects on children.
